analysis.one_liner: Requires union elections by secret ballot and lets employer-raised disputes delay the vote.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the National Labor Relations Act to require that workers choose union representation by secret ballot and to bar an election until the National Labor Relations Board holds a hearing and rules on any dispute an employer or union raises about who can vote or what the bargaining unit is. Secret ballots are already how these elections are run under current board practice, so the practical effect of the bill is to guarantee employers a pre-election legal fight that can postpone the vote. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers facing union organizing drives. The requirement that the board hold a hearing and rule on any employer-raised dispute before an election takes place gives employers a built-in way to push the vote further out, a longer window to campaign against the union, and a chance to challenge the composition of the workforce that would vote.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that any representative chosen for collective bargaining be selected by secret ballot in an election conducted by the National Labor Relations Board.

Bars an election after a petition is filed until the board conducts a hearing and rules on disputes over who is included or excluded from the voting unit and any other legal dispute alleged by the employer or a union seeking recognition, giving employers a mandatory pre-election challenge process.
Sets a one-month deadline for the board to direct an election after a petition is filed, but the pre-election hearing requirement can override that speed in practice.

analysis.who_pays: Workers trying to form a union. A mandatory hearing on every employer-raised dispute delays the election, and a longer campaign period means more time for employer anti-union meetings and pressure before employees finally vote.

drawbacks.text: The mandatory pre-election hearing and ruling requirement would delay union elections whenever an employer raises any legal dispute, extending the period during which employers can hold anti-union meetings and, in practice, in which unlawful retaliation sometimes occurs before employees vote.

Secret ballot elections are already the standard practice in National Labor Relations Board elections, so the bill's headline provision largely codifies the status quo while its real change is the dispute-hearing delay mechanism.
An honest supporter would acknowledge that the one-month election deadline is a genuine speed-up, though the hearing requirement it sits alongside can undo it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The secret ballot guarantee sounds worker-protective but reflects how these elections already work, so the bill's substantive effect is the delay mechanism: any employer can force a hearing that postpones the vote. For workers, the cost of a longer employer campaign period outweighs a ballot change that changes little in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the term ended.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on April 16, 2024, for herself and Republican Senators Tommy Tuberville and Bill Hagerty.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day; that was the only action ever taken.
The bill attracted three cosponsors, all Republicans, and never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers seeking to organize are better off that the bill died, since they avoid a mandatory dispute-hearing process that would lengthen employer campaigns before elections. Employers who preferred the current, faster election rules gained as well, relative to what they would have faced under the bill.

for.name: Sen. Marsha Blackburn
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate labor committee.

for.name: Sens. Tommy Tuberville and Bill Hagerty
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its only additional original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee (Chair Bernie Sanders)
against.role: The committee the bill was referred to and never advanced from
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican (3 total), with no Democratic support, and the Democratic-led committee never moved it.

industries.note: If passed, the bill would give any employer a mandatory pre-election hearing on any legal dispute it raises, delaying the union vote and extending the campaign period during which the employer can press workers against organizing. That gain comes directly at the cost of the workers' choice.

Longer, dispute-laden election timelines expand the market for consultants who advise employers on defeating organizing drives. Their gain runs against workers' interest in a prompt, unpressured vote.
The bill would slow and complicate the election path to representation, costing unions potential members. Their interest here runs alongside the workers who would get the vote sooner.
